content.text: Inspection confirms the application-shell pattern explicitly does not apply to a single-workspace product — a guided phase-gated checklist is the right primary structure. Recording decisions.

avoid: persistent chrome competing with the step in focus
strategy: One step in focus at a time; completed steps collapse to single-line summaries
Generous vertical rhythm and large touch targets on execute/confirm controls
Progressive disclosure: consequence + rollback detail revealed in the confirm gate, not permanently on screen
Single-column reading flow; no dense tables

primary: Runbook progress: phase ladder with per-phase completion
Irreversible-step danger attributes: consequence + rollback plan
secondary: Runbook header: title, owner, change window, overall status

major_choices.choice: Irreversible steps use a typed-phrase confirmation gate that also previews the step's rollback plan before execution
major_choices.rationale: The acceptance seed requires both confirmation AND a recovery path; binding rollback preview into the gate makes 'know the way back' a precondition of proceeding, per P-28 (recovery beats perfect attention)

major_choices.choice: Strict prerequisite gating: a step is locked until earlier steps/checkpoints complete; out-of-order execution is impossible, not merely discouraged
major_choices.rationale: Zero-error completion demands the app make missteps structurally hard (error prevention over error correction)

major_choices.choice: Simulated execution with an append-only activity log; steps carry deterministic mock outcomes
major_choices.rationale: No external services allowed; the product's value is guiding and recording decisions, not performing real infra changes

major_choices.choice: Rollback actions live inside the step (and its gate), reversing exactly the paired irreversible step and logging the recovery
major_choices.rationale: Recovery path must be reachable at the moment of regret, not behind a separate admin surface

primary_structure.pattern: Phase-gated guided checklist (runbook ladder): single-surface wizard-like vertical stepper with locked/unlocked/done step states, a dominant current-step focus region, and a confirm-gate modal for irreversible steps
rationale: Cardinality one + single main screen: one workspace dominates, so PAT-APPLICATION-SHELL's own contract (does_not_apply_when: single workspace) rules it out; PAT-WORKSPACE is excluded for spacious density, so a purpose-fit single-surface guided checklist is used
High hierarchy maps to phase → step nesting rendered as a vertical ladder with phase headers and step rows
Consequential execution maps to wizard-style progression: strict order enforcement makes out-of-order errors structurally impossible (error prevention over error correction)
P-28 Recoverable Action: each irreversible step carries a visible rollback plan previewed inside its confirmation gate
P-26 + H-07: ready/locked/done/blocked states and the audit log are always visible; loading is never a user-visible state because data is inlined
H-01 Task-first entry: first paint shows the runbook title, progress, and the single next actionable step — the task is obvious

rejected.reason: Pattern contract states it does not apply when the product is a single workspace; navigation chrome would dilute the one flow
Tables signal comparison (comparison_need=none) and compress density against the spacious intent; consequences and confirm gates fit poorly in rows
spatiality=none; a diagram implies spatial reasoning that the task does not need
No execution semantics: cannot enforce order, gate irreversibles, or record the audit trail the zero-error success criterion needs

representation.justification_vs_shape: Wizard form factor is the canonical representation for consequential-flow completion: cardinality one (a single path), high hierarchy (phase/step nesting), low comparison (no alternatives shown), medium volatility/uncertainty absorbed by conditional checkpoints and branch notes at the decision points.

primary.reason: A phase-gated wizard-like checklist directly encodes the consequential-flow shape: one path, high hierarchy, strict order, and per-step gates for irreversible actions

rejected.reason: comparison_need none; row density conflicts with spacious intent
shows hierarchy but not progression/gating semantics
read-only; cannot gate or record execution

supporting.reason: Activity log is a flat append-only list of actions/confirmations/rollbacks
Completion summary reads as a short structured document proving zero-error completion

avoid: persistent chrome competing with the step in focus
strategy: One step in focus at a time; completed steps collapse to single-line summaries
Generous vertical rhythm and large targets on execute/confirm controls
Progressive disclosure: consequence + rollback detail revealed in the confirm gate, not permanently on screen
Single-column reading flow; no dense tables

primary: Runbook progress: phase ladder with per-phase completion
Irreversible-step danger attributes: consequence + rollback plan
secondary: Runbook header: title, owner, change window, overall status

major_choices.choice: Irreversible steps use a typed-phrase confirmation gate that previews the step's rollback plan before execution is allowed
major_choices.rationale: The acceptance seed requires both confirmation AND a recovery path; binding rollback preview into the gate makes 'know the way back' a precondition of proceeding, per P-28 Recoverable Action (recovery beats perfect attention)
references: task: complete high-consequence flow with zero errors

major_choices.choice: Strict prerequisite gating: a step stays locked until earlier steps/checkpoints complete; out-of-order execution is structurally impossible, not merely discouraged
major_choices.rationale: Zero-error completion demands the app make missteps structurally hard (error prevention over error correction); the runbook owns order

major_choices.choice: Simulated execution with an append-only activity log; steps carry deterministic mock outcomes and no real side effects
major_choices.rationale: Static single-page delivery with no external services; the product's value is guiding and recording decisions, and the audit log makes zero-error completion verifiable

major_choices.choice: Rollback actions live inside the executed step (and its gate), reversing exactly the paired irreversible step and logging the recovery
major_choices.rationale: The recovery path must be reachable at the moment of regret, not behind a separate admin surface; rollback is user_name 'Rollback plan', always previewable before confirm

primary_structure.pattern: PAT-APPLICATION-SHELL composed down to single-workspace chrome: stable runbook header (title, status, progress) around ONE replaceable work region running a phase-gated guided checklist (runbook ladder) with locked/ready/done step states and a confirm-gate modal for irreversible steps
rationale: The router's only pattern candidate is PAT-APPLICATION-SHELL; its contract composes correctly for this product when multi-area navigation is dropped: keep the stable-chrome force (header/status) and let the work region be the entire runbook ladder — the shell's anti-pattern (backend-table-per-navigation-item) and risk of over-navigation are avoided by having zero nav items
Cardinality one: a single flow dominates, so the work region never swaps; the shell degrades gracefully to header + one workspace
High hierarchy maps to phase → step nesting rendered as a vertical ladder with phase headers and step rows inside the work region

Consequential execution maps to wizard-style progression: strict order enforcement makes out-of-order errors structurally impossible (error prevention over error correction, per task reversibility=irreversible)
P-28 Recoverable Action: each irreversible step carries a rollback plan previewed inside its confirmation gate before execution is possible
P-26 + H-07: ready/locked/done/blocked states and the activity log are always visible; loading is never user-visible because data is inlined at first paint
H-01 Task-first entry: first paint shows runbook title, progress, and the single next actionable step — the task is obvious immediately
WEB-DESKTOP profile: pointer+keyboard, large viewport, generous spacing

rejected.option: Full application shell with multiple global navigation areas
rejected.reason: Contract's does_not_apply_when: single workspace; over-navigation risk with zero secondary areas to navigate
Tables signal comparison (comparison_need=none) and compress density against spacious intent; confirm gates fit poorly in rows
spatiality=none; diagram implies spatial reasoning the task does not need
No execution semantics: cannot enforce order, gate irreversibles, or record the audit trail zero-error success needs

representation.justification_vs_shape: A guided-checklist wizard inside single-workspace chrome is the canonical representation for consequential-flow completion: cardinality one (a single path), high hierarchy (phase/step nesting), no comparison (no alternatives shown), medium volatility/uncertainty absorbed by conditional checkpoints and branch notes at decision points.

primary.reason: A phase-gated wizard-like checklist directly encodes the consequential-flow shape: one path, high hierarchy, strict order, per-step gates for irreversible actions

rejected.reason: comparison_need none; row density conflicts with spacious intent
shows hierarchy but not progression/gating semantics
read-only; cannot gate or record execution

supporting.reason: Activity log is a flat append-only list of actions/confirmations/rollbacks
Completion summary reads as a short structured document proving zero-error completion

content.thinking:
The SDIR linter requires role/behavior_intent/interaction_intents to use known semantic vocabulary (from a controlled vocabulary), OR be prefixed with "experimental:" to mark custom vocabulary. The simplest path: prefix each custom phrase with "experimental:".

So role: "experimental:Runbook identity: title, owner, change window, overall status meter" etc. And behavior_intent items: "experimental:Strict order: ...". interaction_intents likewise.

Let me resubmit with all custom strings prefixed with "experimental:".

content.text: The SDIR linter requires custom vocabulary to be marked `experimental:`. Prefixing all custom phrases and resubmitting.

acceptance: Irreversible steps have a visible confirmation path (gate stating consequence, requiring deliberate typed confirmation) AND a recovery path (documented rollback plan, previewable before confirm, executable after)
First paint shows the full runbook with all data inlined; no loading state is ever user-visible
Steps enforce strict order: locked steps cannot be executed; checkpoints must be satisfied before their dependent step unlocks
Completion requires every step done; the completion summary proves zero-error completion with the audit trail
Single main screen; deliverable opens statically from root index.html with no backend and no external services

adapter_may_choose: typed-phrase confirmation vs checkbox + explicit confirm button
modal interrupt vs inline expansion of the step
decision_points.question: How does the confirm gate for irreversible steps demand deliberation while previewing the rollback plan?

adapter_may_choose: precomputed deterministic condition results
user-declared branch choice recorded in the audit log
decision_points.question: How do conditional checkpoints express medium volatility/uncertainty (conditions that may pass or fail)?

adapter_may_choose: always-visible side region
toggleable drawer/panel
decision_points.question: Is the append-only activity log permanent or toggled?

intent.primary_task: Complete the cutover runbook end-to-end with zero errors, confirming every irreversible step and using its rollback path when needed
secondary_tasks: Review consequence and rollback plan before executing an irreversible step
Reset the runbook for another rehearsal

interaction_intents: experimental:Execute a reversible step (check-off with recorded outcome)
experimental:Execute an irreversible step through the confirm gate (typed confirmation; rollback preview shown first)
experimental:Trigger a documented rollback for an executed irreversible step (logged as recovery)
experimental:Expand/collapse phase and step rows; the single next actionable step is emphasized
experimental:Open/close the activity log
experimental:Reset the runbook to its initial state (session-local rehearsal)

behavior_intent: experimental:Show overall progress (steps done / total) and runbook state (not started / in progress / complete)
experimental:Never swaps; the work region owns all change
regions.role: experimental:Runbook identity: title, owner, change window, overall status meter

behavior_intent: experimental:Strict order: each step locked until prerequisites complete
experimental:Irreversible steps carry a persistent warning badge and differ visually from reversible checks
experimental:Completed steps collapse to one-line summaries with their recorded outcome
experimental:Current step expanded with full detail and its action control
regions.role: experimental:Hierarchical phase/step checklist: phases as sections, steps as rows with locked/ready/done states; current step expanded with detail and action controls

behavior_intent: experimental:State the consequence explicitly before any commit
experimental:Show the paired rollback plan before the confirm input is enabled
experimental:Require typed phrase matching the step's confirm phrase
experimental:Cancel always returns to the ladder with nothing changed
regions.role: experimental:Modal interrupt for irreversible execution: consequence statement, rollback plan preview, typed-phrase confirmation, cancel path

behavior_intent: experimental:Append-only; entries are never edited or removed
experimental:Latest entries readable at a glance; entry types: executed, confirmed, rolled back, reset
regions.role: experimental:Append-only audit trail of executions, confirmations, rollbacks, and resets with timestamps

behavior_intent: experimental:Enumerate all steps with outcomes and confirmation/rollback records
experimental:Link to the full audit trail
experimental:Persist until reset
regions.role: experimental:Zero-error completion proof shown when the final step completes: per-phase outcome roll-up and audit highlights

primary.reason: Phase-gated wizard-like checklist inside single-workspace chrome encodes one path, high hierarchy, strict order, and per-step gates

supporting.reason: Append-only audit entries
Completion summary reads as a structured proof document

user_job.success: walked the full flow with zero errors; every irreversible step confirmed with a usable recovery path

1. **Preflight** (reversible checks)
   - S1: Confirm change window & freeze (checklist; reversible)
   - S2: Verify replication lag & backups (reversible) — includes a conditional checkpoint (uncertainty): backup freshness check that can be "ok" 
   - S3: Announce maintenance start in status page (reversible)

2. **Cutover**
   - S4: Enable maintenance mode (irreversible? maintenance mode is reversible... make it irreversible-ish: "Drain in-flight writes" — irreversible? Draining is reversible-ish. Better irreversible examples:
   - S4: Deploy ledger v2 binaries to canary (reversible? rollback = redeploy v1; classify as reversible check with outcome)
   - S5: **Cut over write traffic to Ledger v2** (irreversible — typed confirm, rollback plan: "Fail write traffic back to v1 and revert DNS within 30 min")
   - S6: **Revoke v1 write credentials** (irreversible — deeper point of no return; rollback: "Reissue credentials from break-glass vault")

3. **Verification**
   - S7: Verify transaction success rate (reversible, conditional: threshold check)
   - S8: **Decommission v1 fleet** (irreversible — rollback: "Restore v1 fleet from golden image (RTO 45 min)")

4. **Closeout**
   - S9: Resume traffic & close window (reversible)
   - S10: Publish cutover report (reversible)

Hmm — keep 4 phases, ~10 steps. That's a good volume: medium, low density. Each step has: id, title, description, reversible bool, checkpoints (list of prerequisite conditions: e.g., requires prior steps; plus inline safety checks user must tick?), outcome (deterministic simulated result), consequence text (irreversible), rollback plan (title, steps, rto), confirmPhrase (e.g., "CUTOVER WRITES").

Gating model:
- Each step has `requires`: list of step ids that must be done. Default: previous step in order.
- Conditional checkpoints: some steps have a "condition" that resolves deterministically (e.g., S7 verification: if success rate ≥ threshold → pass). - Step states: locked (prereqs unmet), ready, done. Irreversible done steps show "Rolled back?" no — after execution, irreversible step shows its outcome + a "Roll back" button. # Ledger v2 Cutover — Runbook Walker (cell-j10-s09)

A single-page web app for **completing one high-consequence workflow with zero
errors**: a production cutover runbook. Strict-order execution makes missteps
structurally impossible; every **irreversible** step is behind a typed
confirmation gate that previews its **rollback plan** first, and executed
irreversible steps keep an inline recovery path until a dependent step runs.

## Run

Static — no build, no backend, no external services:

- Open `index.html` directly in a browser (double-click works), **or**
- serve the folder: `python -m http.server 8000` → http://localhost:8000

## What ships in the first paint

All runbook data is inlined in `data.js`; `app.js` renders synchronously at
parse time. There is no loading state — the full ladder (4 phases, 10 steps)
is usable the instant the page opens.

## The flow

1. **Preflight** — reversible checklist steps (some with tick-to-confirm
   checkpoints).
2. **Cutover** — deploy (reversible), then two points of no return:
   *Cut over write traffic* (`LEDGER V2`) and *Revoke v1 credentials*
   (`REVOKE V1`).
3. **Verification** — health checks, then *Decommission v1 fleet*
   (`RETIRE V1`).
4. **Closeout** — close the window, publish the record.

## Safety model (acceptance seed: irreversible steps have recovery/confirmation paths)

- Steps unlock strictly in order; locked steps cannot execute.
- Irreversible steps carry a persistent **Irreversible** badge.
- Executing one opens a **confirm gate**: explicit consequence statement, the
  paired **rollback plan previewed before** you can confirm, two acknowledgement
  checkboxes, and a **typed phrase** that must match.
- After execution, the step keeps an inline **Roll back** button (two-click
  confirm) — usable until a dependent step has executed, at which point the
  window closes and the UI says so honestly.
- Every action appends to the **activity log** (append-only during a run);
  completion shows a zero-misstep summary with gate/rollback/audit counts.

State is session-local by design (no persistence service in scope); reset
re-arms a fresh rehearsal.

## Files

| File | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `index.html` | Screen shell + regions (header, ladder, gate, log, completion) |
| `styles.css` | Design tokens + layout (spacious, WCAG-AA contrast, focus-visible) |
| `data.js` | Inlined runbook (phases, steps, checkpoints, consequences, rollback plans) |
| `app.js` | State machine: gating, confirm gate, rollback, audit log, render |

Fix: add `visibility: hidden` when closed → removes from tab order and from a11y tree: .log-drawer { visibility: hidden; transition: transform .25s ease, visibility 0s .25s; } .log-drawer.open { visibility: visible; transition: transform .25s ease; }.

Then completion (hidden), ladder steps... first ladder focusable is step-row button, then checkboxes... That's fine sequence-wise.

---
name: prax-gate-vocabulary-quirks
description: Prax design MCP gates demand exact routed pattern IDs, known-reference citations, experimental: prefix for custom SDIR vocab, and run their own browser a11y checks on validate
metadata:
  type: project
---

Prax (`mcp__prax__design_*`, project `.mcp.json` in the pi-matrix benchmark worktrees) has strict machine-checked gate contracts that cost retries when guessed:

- `design_decide`: `primary_structure.pattern` must be a pattern ID **returned by `design_route`** (exact ID match, not a string containing it) and inspected via `design_inspect` to ≥L1. `major_choices[].references` must cite **known** concepts only — product-object ids from the frame, exact task strings, or context entities; free-form phrases fail with MAJOR_CHOICE_REFERENCE_UNKNOWN. `design_route` is illegal outside the ROUTING gate (session-phase enforced).
- `design_sdir`: almost all fields nest under `screen` (including `user_job`, `acceptance`, `state_ownership`); `priority.primary/contextual` must list **region ids**; `state_ownership.owner` must be a region id, `session`, or `url`; any custom role/behavior/interaction phrase must be prefixed `experimental:` or it fails SDIR_UNKNOWN_VOCABULARY.
- `design_validate` (evaluate, no receipts): Prax **drives a real browser itself** (viewport ~1280x860) and returns `measurement_feedback` per-check failures with 3 measure rounds. It enforces WCAG AA: `opacity` on containers breaks text-contrast measurement (use solid dim colors), off-screen drawers must be `visibility:hidden` when closed or focus_order fails, checkboxes ≥24px or target_size fails. White-on-button text needs ≥4.5:1 (e.g. `#3730a3`, not `#4338ca`).
- `design_prepare_implementation`: `framework` is const `react` (advisory brief even for vanilla implementations); `measurement_target.entry` must be a root-relative URL path (`/index.html`).

**Why:** the gates are enforced by schema+lint, not judgment; knowing the exact accepted vocabulary avoids EXPAND/RETRY loops.
**How to apply:** in Prax sessions, reuse routed IDs verbatim, prefix custom vocab, nest SDIR fields under `screen`, and pre-harden CSS against the a11y triplet before the first evaluate call.

Base directory for this skill: C:\Users\SiChuchen\.claude\plugins\cache\superpowers-marketplace\superpowers-chrome\3.0.1\skills\browsing

# Browsing with Chrome Direct

## Overview

Control Chrome via DevTools Protocol using the `use_browser` MCP tool. Single unified interface with auto-starting Chrome.

**Announce:** "I'm using the browsing skill to control Chrome."

## When to Use

**Use this when:**
- Controlling authenticated sessions
- Managing multiple tabs in running browser
- Playwright MCP unavailable or excessive

**Use Playwright MCP when:**
- Need fresh browser instances
- Generating screenshots/PDFs
- Prefer higher-level abstractions

## Auto-Capture

Every DOM action (navigate, click, type, select, eval, keyboard_press, hover, drag_drop, double_click, right_click, file_upload) automatically saves:
- `{prefix}.png` — viewport screenshot
- `{prefix}.md` — page content as structured markdown
- `{prefix}.html` — full rendered DOM
- `{prefix}-console.txt` — browser console messages

Files are saved to the session directory with sequential prefixes (001-navigate, 002-click, etc.). You must check these before using extract or screenshot actions.

## The use_browser Tool

Single MCP tool with action-based interface. Chrome auto-starts on first use.

**Parameters:**
- `action` (required): Operation to perform
- `selector` (optional): CSS or XPath selector for element operations
- `payload` (optional): Action-specific data (string or object)
- `timeout` (optional): Timeout in ms for await operations (default: 5000)

**Active tab**: Every action operates on the current `activeTab`. Use `switch_tab` to change it.

## Actions Reference

### Navigation
- **navigate**: Navigate to URL
  - `payload`: URL string
  - Example: `{action: "navigate", payload: "https://example.com"}`

- **await_element**: Wait for element to appear
  - `selector`: CSS selector
  - `timeout`: Max wait time in ms
  - Example: `{action: "await_element", selector: ".loaded", timeout: 10000}`

- **await_text**: Wait for text to appear
  - `payload`: Text to wait for
  - Example: `{action: "await_text", payload: "Welcome"}`

### Interaction
- **click**: Click element
  - `selector`: CSS selector
  - Example: `{action: "click", selector: "button.submit"}`

- **type**: Text input
  - `selector`: Optional — clicks to focus first
  - `payload`: Text to type (`\t`=Tab, `\n`=Enter)
  - Example: `{action: "type", selector: "#email", payload: "user@example.com"}`

- **double_click**: Double-click element (fires dblclick event)
  - `selector`: CSS selector
  - Example: `{action: "double_click", selector: ".item"}`

- **right_click**: Right-click element (fires contextmenu event)
  - `selector`: CSS selector
  - Example: `{action: "right_click", selector: ".row"}`

- **select**: Select dropdown option
  - `selector`: CSS selector
  - `payload`: Option value(s)
  - Example: `{action: "select", selector: "select[name=state]", payload: "CA"}`

- **keyboard_press**: Press special keys (Tab, Enter, Escape, Arrow keys, F1-F12)
  - `payload`: Key name (string) or `{"key": "Tab", "modifiers": {"shift": true, "ctrl": false, "alt": false, "meta": false}}`
  - Example: `{action: "keyboard_press", payload: "Tab"}`
  - Example with modifiers: `{action: "keyboard_press", payload: {"key": "Tab", "modifiers": {"shift": true}}}`

### Mouse Actions (CDP-Level)
These use CDP Input.dispatchMouseEvent, bypassing synthetic event restrictions.

- **hover**: Move mouse over element (CSS :hover, tooltips, menus)
  - `selector`: CSS selector
  - Example: `{action: "hover", selector: ".menu-trigger"}`

- **drag_drop**: Drag element to target (native drag-and-drop via CDP)
  - `selector`: Source element
  - `payload`: Target selector or JSON coordinates `{"x":N,"y":N}`
  - Example: `{action: "drag_drop", selector: ".card", payload: ".column-2"}`

- **mouse_move**: Move mouse to coordinates
  - `payload`: JSON `{"x":N,"y":N}` (optional: `steps`, `fromX`, `fromY` for smooth movement)
  - Example: `{action: "mouse_move", payload: "{\"x\":100,\"y\":200}"}`

- **scroll**: Scroll via mouse wheel events
  - `payload`: Direction (up/down/left/right) or JSON `{"deltaX":N,"deltaY":N}`
  - `selector`: Optional — scroll within element
  - Example: `{action: "scroll", payload: "down"}`

### File Upload
- **file_upload**: Set files on input[type=file] elements (can't be done via JavaScript)
  - `selector`: File input element
  - `payload`: File path or JSON `{"files":["/path/a.pdf","/path/b.jpg"]}`
  - Example: `{action: "file_upload", selector: "#upload", payload: "/tmp/doc.pdf"}`

### Extraction
- **extract**: Get page content
  - `payload`: Format ('markdown'|'text'|'html')
  - `selector`: Optional - limit to element
  - Example: `{action: "extract", payload: "markdown"}`
  - Example: `{action: "extract", payload: "text", selector: "h1"}`

- **attr**: Get element attribute
  - `selector`: CSS selector
  - `payload`: Attribute name
  - Example: `{action: "attr", selector: "a.download", payload: "href"}`

- **eval**: Execute JavaScript
  - `payload`: JavaScript code
  - Example: `{action: "eval", payload: "document.title"}`

### Export
- **screenshot**: Capture screenshot of a specific element
  - `payload`: Filename
  - `selector`: Optional - screenshot specific element
  - Viewport screenshots are auto-captured after every DOM action. Use this only when you need a specific element.
  - Example: `{action: "screenshot", payload: "/tmp/chart.png", selector: ".chart"}`

### Tab Management
- **list_tabs**: List all open tabs
  - Example: `{action: "list_tabs"}`

- **new_tab**: Create new tab
  - Example: `{action: "new_tab"}`

- **close_tab**: Close the active tab
  - Example: `{action: "close_tab"}`

- **switch_tab**: Switch the active tab (sticky — stays until changed)
  - `payload`: Tab index (number), URL substring, or title substring
  - Example: `{action: "switch_tab", payload: 1}` (by index)
  - Example: `{action: "switch_tab", payload: "example.com"}` (by URL substring)
  - Example: `{action: "switch_tab", payload: "GitHub"}` (by title substring)

### Browser Mode Control
- **show_browser**: Make browser window visible (headed mode)
  - Example: `{action: "show_browser"}`
  - ⚠️ **WARNING**: Restarts Chrome, reloads pages via GET, loses POST state

- **hide_browser**: Switch to headless mode (invisible browser)
  - Example: `{action: "hide_browser"}`
  - ⚠️ **WARNING**: Restarts Chrome, reloads pages via GET, loses POST state

- **browser_mode**: Check current browser mode, port, and profile
  - Example: `{action: "browser_mode"}`
  - Returns: `{"headless": true|false, "mode": "headless"|"headed", "running": true|false, "port": 9222, "profile": "name", "profileDir": "/path"}`

### Profile Management
- **set_profile**: Change Chrome profile (must kill Chrome first)
  - Example: `{action: "set_profile", "payload": "browser-user"}`
  - ⚠️ **WARNING**: Chrome must be stopped first
  - **Side effect**: marks the profile as explicit, opting out of auto-disambiguation (see below)

- **get_profile**: Get current profile name and directory
  - Example: `{action: "get_profile"}`
  - Returns: `{"profile": "name", "profileDir": "/path"}`

**Default behavior**: Chrome starts in **headless mode** with **"superpowers-chrome" profile** on a **dynamically allocated port** (range 9222-12111). Override the port with `CHROME_WS_PORT`; override the profile with `CHROME_WS_PROFILE`.

**Auto-disambiguation across parallel MCPs**:
When two MCP servers start on the same host with the default profile, the first claims `superpowers-chrome` (port 9222) and later ones silently fall through to `superpowers-chrome-2` (port 9223), `superpowers-chrome-3`, etc. Each MCP drives its own Chrome with its own profile dir; they don't fight over `activeTab`. The bridge tracks ownership via a lock file at `~/.cache/superpowers/browser-profiles/<profile>.mcp.lock`; stale locks (dead PIDs) are reclaimed automatically.

To opt **out** of disambiguation — e.g., to intentionally share Chrome between a long-lived `chrome-ws` CLI session and your MCP — set the profile name explicitly:
- Env var: `CHROME_WS_PROFILE=my-profile`
- Or: `{action: "set_profile", payload: "my-profile"}` at runtime

An explicit profile name still acquires the lock, but on conflict the bridge **shares** rather than disambiguates — the second process reconnects to the first's Chrome (the original reconnect-on-restart behavior).

### Chrome Lifecycle (Recovery)
- **kill_chrome**: Kill the Chrome process this MCP is driving
  - Example: `{action: "kill_chrome"}`
  - Releases the meta.json; next page action auto-restarts Chrome

- **restart_chrome**: kill_chrome + immediate spawn
  - Example: `{action: "restart_chrome"}`

**Auto-restart banner**: when the bridge has to spawn a fresh Chrome (because the previous one died or was killed externally — e.g., `kill -9 <pid>` from the shell), the first response after the restart prepends:
```
[Chrome auto-restarted; URL reset to about:blank. Re-navigate to continue.]
```
Treat this as a signal that your prior URL / tab state is gone — re-navigate before assuming anything about the current page.

### Console Logging
Capture browser console output for the active tab. Buffer is keyed by the page session's `sessionId`, so it survives `close_tab`/`new_tab` ordering quirks. Levels: `log`, `info`, `warn`, `error`.

- **enable_console_logging**: Start capturing
  - Example: `{action: "enable_console_logging"}`

- **get_console_messages**: Read captured messages
  - All: `{action: "get_console_messages"}`
  - Since timestamp (epoch ms): `{action: "get_console_messages", payload: {since: 1716000000000}}`
  - Returns: array of `{timestamp, level, text}` entries

- **clear_console_messages**: Reset the buffer
  - Example: `{action: "clear_console_messages"}`

### Dialog Handling
Native dialogs (JS alert/confirm/prompt, beforeunload, HTTP basic-auth, permission prompts, device choosers) pause the page. While a dialog is open, page-targeted actions (`extract`, `click`, `eval`, etc.) return a refusal whose text contains `Page is behind a dialog` and lists the available `dialog::*` selectors.

- `{prefix}.png` — viewport screenshot
- `{prefix}.md` — page content as structured markdown
- `{prefix}.html` — full rendered DOM

Single MCP tool with action-based interface. Chrome auto-starts on first use.

- `action` (required): Operation to perform
- `selector` (optional): CSS or XPath selector for element operations

  - `selector`: CSS selector
  - `timeout`: Max wait time in ms
  - Example: `{action: "await_element", selector: ".loaded", timeout: 10000}`

  - `payload`: Text to wait for

  - `selector`: CSS selector

  - `selector`: Optional — clicks to focus first
  - `payload`: Text to type (`\t`=Tab, `\n`=Enter)
  - Example: `{action: "type", selector: "#email", payload: "user@example.com"}`

- **double_click**: Double-click element (fires dblclick event)

  - Example: `{action: "double_click", selector: ".item"}`

  - `selector`: CSS selector
  - Example: `{action: "right_click", selector: ".row"}`

  - `payload`: Option value(s)

# Browsing with Chrome Direct

## Overview

Control Chrome via DevTools Protocol using the `use_browser` MCP tool. Single unified interface with auto-starting Chrome.

**Announce:** "I'm using the browsing skill to control Chrome."

## When to Use

**Use this when:**
- Controlling authenticated sessions
- Managing multiple tabs in running browser
- Playwright MCP unavailable or excessive

**Use Playwright MCP when:**
- Need fresh browser instances
- Generating screenshots/PDFs
- Prefer higher-level abstractions

## Auto-Capture

Every DOM action (navigate, click, type, select, eval, keyboard_press, hover, drag_drop, double_click, right_click, file_upload) automatically saves:
- `{prefix}.png` — viewport screenshot
- `{prefix}.md` — page content as structured markdown
- `{prefix}.html` — full rendered DOM
- `{prefix}-console.txt` — browser console messages

Files are saved to the session directory with sequential prefixes (001-navigate, 002-click, etc.). You must check these before using extract or screenshot actions.

## The use_browser Tool

Single MCP tool with action-based interface. Chrome auto-starts on first use.

**Parameters:**
- `action` (required): Operation to perform
- `selector` (optional): CSS or XPath selector for element operations
- `payload` (optional): Action-specific data (string or object)
- `timeout` (optional): Timeout in ms for await operations (default: 5000)

**Active tab**: Every action operates on the current `activeTab`. Use `switch_tab` to change it.

## Actions Reference

### Navigation
- **navigate**: Navigate to URL
  - `payload`: URL string
  - Example: `{action: "navigate", payload: "https://example.com"}`

- **await_element**: Wait for element to appear
  - `selector`: CSS selector
  - `timeout`: Max wait time in ms
  - Example: `{action: "await_element", selector: ".loaded", timeout: 10000}`

- **await_text**: Wait for text to appear
  - `payload`: Text to wait for
  - Example: `{action: "await_text", payload: "Welcome"}`

### Interaction
- **click**: Click element
  - `selector`: CSS selector
  - Example: `{action: "click", selector: "button.submit"}`

- **type**: Text input
  - `selector`: Optional — clicks to focus first
  - `payload`: Text to type (`\t`=Tab, `\n`=Enter)
  - Example: `{action: "type", selector: "#email", payload: "user@example.com"}`

- **double_click**: Double-click element (fires dblclick event)
  - `selector`: CSS selector
  - Example: `{action: "double_click", selector: ".item"}`

- **right_click**: Right-click element (fires contextmenu event)
  - `selector`: CSS selector
  - Example: `{action: "right_click", selector: ".row"}`

- **select**: Select dropdown option
  - `selector`: CSS selector
  - `payload`: Option value(s)
  - Example: `{action: "select", selector: "select[name=state]", payload: "CA"}`

- **keyboard_press**: Press special keys (Tab, Enter, Escape, Arrow keys, F1-F12)
  - `payload`: Key name (string) or `{"key": "Tab", "modifiers": {"shift": true, "ctrl": false, "alt": false, "meta": false}}`
  - Example: `{action: "keyboard_press", payload: "Tab"}`
  - Example with modifiers: `{action: "keyboard_press", payload: {"key": "Tab", "modifiers": {"shift": true}}}`

### Mouse Actions (CDP-Level)
These use CDP Input.dispatchMouseEvent, bypassing synthetic event restrictions.

- **hover**: Move mouse over element (CSS :hover, tooltips, menus)
  - `selector`: CSS selector
  - Example: `{action: "hover", selector: ".menu-trigger"}`

- **drag_drop**: Drag element to target (native drag-and-drop via CDP)
  - `selector`: Source element
  - `payload`: Target selector or JSON coordinates `{"x":N,"y":N}`
  - Example: `{action: "drag_drop", selector: ".card", payload: ".column-2"}`

- **mouse_move**: Move mouse to coordinates
  - `payload`: JSON `{"x":N,"y":N}` (optional: `steps`, `fromX`, `fromY` for smooth movement)
  - Example: `{action: "mouse_move", payload: "{\"x\":100,\"y\":200}"}`

- **scroll**: Scroll via mouse wheel events
  - `payload`: Direction (up/down/left/right) or JSON `{"deltaX":N,"deltaY":N}`
  - `selector`: Optional — scroll within element
  - Example: `{action: "scroll", payload: "down"}`

### File Upload
- **file_upload**: Set files on input[type=file] elements (can't be done via JavaScript)
  - `selector`: File input element
  - `payload`: File path or JSON `{"files":["/path/a.pdf","/path/b.jpg"]}`
  - Example: `{action: "file_upload", selector: "#upload", payload: "/tmp/doc.pdf"}`

### Extraction
- **extract**: Get page content
  - `payload`: Format ('markdown'|'text'|'html')
  - `selector`: Optional - limit to element
  - Example: `{action: "extract", payload: "markdown"}`
  - Example: `{action: "extract", payload: "text", selector: "h1"}`

- **attr**: Get element attribute
  - `selector`: CSS selector
  - `payload`: Attribute name
  - Example: `{action: "attr", selector: "a.download", payload: "href"}`

- **eval**: Execute JavaScript
  - `payload`: JavaScript code
  - Example: `{action: "eval", payload: "document.title"}`

### Export
- **screenshot**: Capture screenshot of a specific element
  - `payload`: Filename
  - `selector`: Optional - screenshot specific element
  - Viewport screenshots are auto-captured after every DOM action. Use this only when you need a specific element.
  - Example: `{action: "screenshot", payload: "/tmp/chart.png", selector: ".chart"}`

### Tab Management
- **list_tabs**: List all open tabs
  - Example: `{action: "list_tabs"}`

- **new_tab**: Create new tab
  - Example: `{action: "new_tab"}`

- **close_tab**: Close the active tab
  - Example: `{action: "close_tab"}`

- **switch_tab**: Switch the active tab (sticky — stays until changed)
  - `payload`: Tab index (number), URL substring, or title substring
  - Example: `{action: "switch_tab", payload: 1}` (by index)
  - Example: `{action: "switch_tab", payload: "example.com"}` (by URL substring)
  - Example: `{action: "switch_tab", payload: "GitHub"}` (by title substring)

### Browser Mode Control
- **show_browser**: Make browser window visible (headed mode)
  - Example: `{action: "show_browser"}`
  - ⚠️ **WARNING**: Restarts Chrome, reloads pages via GET, loses POST state

- **hide_browser**: Switch to headless mode (invisible browser)
  - Example: `{action: "hide_browser"}`
  - ⚠️ **WARNING**: Restarts Chrome, reloads pages via GET, loses POST state

- **browser_mode**: Check current browser mode, port, and profile
  - Example: `{action: "browser_mode"}`
  - Returns: `{"headless": true|false, "mode": "headless"|"headed", "running": true|false, "port": 9222, "profile": "name", "profileDir": "/path"}`

### Profile Management
- **set_profile**: Change Chrome profile (must kill Chrome first)
  - Example: `{action: "set_profile", "payload": "browser-user"}`
  - ⚠️ **WARNING**: Chrome must be stopped first
  - **Side effect**: marks the profile as explicit, opting out of auto-disambiguation (see below)

- **get_profile**: Get current profile name and directory
  - Example: `{action: "get_profile"}`
  - Returns: `{"profile": "name", "profileDir": "/path"}`

**Default behavior**: Chrome starts in **headless mode** with **"superpowers-chrome" profile** on a **dynamically allocated port** (range 9222-12111). Override the port with `CHROME_WS_PORT`; override the profile with `CHROME_WS_PROFILE`.

**Auto-disambiguation across parallel MCPs**:
When two MCP servers start on the same host with the default profile, the first claims `superpowers-chrome` (port 9222) and later ones silently fall through to `superpowers-chrome-2` (port 9223), `superpowers-chrome-3`, etc. Each MCP drives its own Chrome with its own profile dir; they don't fight over `activeTab`. The bridge tracks ownership via a lock file at `~/.cache/superpowers/browser-profiles/<profile>.mcp.lock`; stale locks (dead PIDs) are reclaimed automatically.

To opt **out** of disambiguation — e.g., to intentionally share Chrome between a long-lived `chrome-ws` CLI session and your MCP — set the profile name explicitly:
- Env var: `CHROME_WS_PROFILE=my-profile`
- Or: `{action: "set_profile", payload: "my-profile"}` at runtime

An explicit profile name still acquires the lock, but on conflict the bridge **shares** rather than disambiguates — the second process reconnects to the first's Chrome (the original reconnect-on-restart behavior).

### Chrome Lifecycle (Recovery)
- **kill_chrome**: Kill the Chrome process this MCP is driving
  - Example: `{action: "kill_chrome"}`
  - Releases the meta.json; next page action auto-restarts Chrome

- **restart_chrome**: kill_chrome + immediate spawn
  - Example: `{action: "restart_chrome"}`

**Auto-restart banner**: when the bridge has to spawn a fresh Chrome (because the previous one died or was killed externally — e.g., `kill -9 <pid>` from the shell), the first response after the restart prepends:
```
[Chrome auto-restarted; URL reset to about:blank. Re-navigate to continue.]
```
Treat this as a signal that your prior URL / tab state is gone — re-navigate before assuming anything about the current page.

### Console Logging
Capture browser console output for the active tab. Buffer is keyed by the page session's `sessionId`, so it survives `close_tab`/`new_tab` ordering quirks. Levels: `log`, `info`, `warn`, `error`.

- **enable_console_logging**: Start capturing
  - Example: `{action: "enable_console_logging"}`

- **get_console_messages**: Read captured messages
  - All: `{action: "get_console_messages"}`
  - Since timestamp (epoch ms): `{action: "get_console_messages", payload: {since: 1716000000000}}`
  - Returns: array of `{timestamp, level, text}` entries

- **clear_console_messages**: Reset the buffer
  - Example: `{action: "clear_console_messages"}`

### Dialog Handling
Native dialogs (JS alert/confirm/prompt, beforeunload, HTTP basic-auth, permission prompts, device choosers) pause the page. While a dialog is open, page-targeted actions (`extract`, `click`, `eval`, etc.) return a refusal whose text contains `Page is behind a dialog` and lists the available `dialog::*` selectors.

When a dialog fires **during** a `navigate` (typical for HTTP basic-auth), `navigate` itself throws with the dialog grammar in the message — you don't have to issue a separate page-targeted call to discover the dialog.

Handle dialogs by clicking/typing a `dialog::*` selector:
- `{action: "click", selector: "dialog::accept"}` — accept JS alert/confirm/prompt, beforeunload, permission grant
- `{action: "click", selector: "dialog::dismiss"}` — dismiss / cancel / deny
- `{action: "type", selector: "dialog::prompt", payload: "text"}` then accept — respond to JS prompt
- `{action: "type", selector: "dialog::username", payload: "alice"}` + `{action: "type", selector: "dialog::password", payload: "secret"}` + `{action: "click", selector: "dialog::accept"}` — HTTP basic-auth
- `{action: "click", selector: "dialog::device[id=\"<deviceId>\"]"}` — pick a WebUSB/Bluetooth/Serial/HID device

**Critical caveats when toggling modes**:
1. **Chrome must restart** - Cannot switch headless/headed mode on running Chrome
2. **Pages reload via GET** - All open tabs are reopened with GET requests
3. **POST state is lost** - Form submissions, POST results, and POST-based navigation will be lost
4. **Session state is lost** - Any client-side state (JavaScript variables, etc.) is cleared
5. **Cookies/auth may persist** - Uses same user data directory, so logged-in sessions may survive

**When to use headed mode**:
- Debugging visual rendering issues
- Demonstrating browser behavior to user
- Testing features that only work with visible browser
- Debugging issues that don't reproduce in headless mode

**When to stay in headless mode** (default):
- All other cases - faster, cleaner, less intrusive
- Screenshots work perfectly in headless mode
- Most automation works identically in both modes

**Profile management**:
Profiles store persistent browser data (cookies, localStorage, extensions, auth sessions).

**Profile locations**:
- macOS: `~/Library/Caches/superpowers/browser-profiles/{name}/`
- Linux: `~/.cache/superpowers/browser-profiles/{name}/`
- Windows: `%LOCALAPPDATA%/superpowers/browser-profiles/{name}/`

**When to use separate profiles**:
- **Default profile ("superpowers-chrome")**: General automation, shared sessions
- **Agent-specific profiles**: Isolate different agents' browser state
  - Example: browser-user agent uses "browser-user" profile
- **Task-specific profiles**: Testing with different user contexts
  - Example: "test-logged-in" vs "test-logged-out"

**Profile data persists across**:
- Chrome restarts
- Mode toggles (headless ↔ headed)
- System reboots (data is in cache directory)

**To use a different profile**:
1. Kill Chrome if running: `await chromeLib.killChrome()`
2. Set profile: `{action: "set_profile", "payload": "my-profile"}`
3. Start Chrome: Next navigate/action will use new profile

## Quick Start Pattern

Navigate and extract:
{action: "navigate", payload: "https://example.com"}
{action: "await_element", selector: "h1"}
{action: "extract", payload: "text", selector: "h1"}
```

```
{action: "navigate", payload: "https://example.com/login"}
{action: "await_element", selector: "input[name=email]"}
{action: "type", selector: "input[name=email]", payload: "user@example.com"}

{action: "await_text", payload: "Welcome"}

2. **Use chrome-ws to verify** - Test the same operation via CLI
3. **Adapt the pattern** - Apply the working CDP approach to use_browser

- **Form validation**: Fill forms, check error states
- **UI state testing**: Click elements, verify DOM changes
- **Performance testing**: Measure load times, capture metrics
- **Screenshot comparison**: Capture before/after states

# Browsing with Chrome Direct

## Overview

Control Chrome via DevTools Protocol using the `use_browser` MCP tool. Single unified interface with auto-starting Chrome.

**Announce:** "I'm using the browsing skill to control Chrome."

## When to Use

**Use this when:**
- Controlling authenticated sessions
- Managing multiple tabs in running browser
- Playwright MCP unavailable or excessive

**Use Playwright MCP when:**
- Need fresh browser instances
- Generating screenshots/PDFs
- Prefer higher-level abstractions

## Auto-Capture

Every DOM action (navigate, click, type, select, eval, keyboard_press, hover, drag_drop, double_click, right_click, file_upload) automatically saves:
- `{prefix}.png` — viewport screenshot
- `{prefix}.md` — page content as structured markdown
- `{prefix}.html` — full rendered DOM
- `{prefix}-console.txt` — browser console messages

Files are saved to the session directory with sequential prefixes (001-navigate, 002-click, etc.). You must check these before using extract or screenshot actions.

## The use_browser Tool

Single MCP tool with action-based interface. Chrome auto-starts on first use.

**Parameters:**
- `action` (required): Operation to perform
- `selector` (optional): CSS or XPath selector for element operations
- `payload` (optional): Action-specific data (string or object)
- `timeout` (optional): Timeout in ms for await operations (default: 5000)

**Active tab**: Every action operates on the current `activeTab`. Use `switch_tab` to change it.

## Actions Reference

### Navigation
- **navigate**: Navigate to URL
  - `payload`: URL string
  - Example: `{action: "navigate", payload: "https://example.com"}`

- **await_element**: Wait for element to appear
  - `selector`: CSS selector
  - `timeout`: Max wait time in ms
  - Example: `{action: "await_element", selector: ".loaded", timeout: 10000}`

- **await_text**: Wait for text to appear
  - `payload`: Text to wait for
  - Example: `{action: "await_text", payload: "Welcome"}`

### Interaction
- **click**: Click element
  - `selector`: CSS selector
  - Example: `{action: "click", selector: "button.submit"}`

- **type**: Text input
  - `selector`: Optional — clicks to focus first
  - `payload`: Text to type (`\t`=Tab, `\n`=Enter)
  - Example: `{action: "type", selector: "#email", payload: "user@example.com"}`

- **double_click**: Double-click element (fires dblclick event)
  - `selector`: CSS selector
  - Example: `{action: "double_click", selector: ".item"}`

- **right_click**: Right-click element (fires contextmenu event)
  - `selector`: CSS selector
  - Example: `{action: "right_click", selector: ".row"}`

- **select**: Select dropdown option
  - `selector`: CSS selector
  - `payload`: Option value(s)
  - Example: `{action: "select", selector: "select[name=state]", payload: "CA"}`

- **keyboard_press**: Press special keys (Tab, Enter, Escape, Arrow keys, F1-F12)
  - `payload`: Key name (string) or `{"key": "Tab", "modifiers": {"shift": true, "ctrl": false, "alt": false, "meta": false}}`
  - Example: `{action: "keyboard_press", payload: "Tab"}`
  - Example with modifiers: `{action: "keyboard_press", payload: {"key": "Tab", "modifiers": {"shift": true}}}`

### Mouse Actions (CDP-Level)
These use CDP Input.dispatchMouseEvent, bypassing synthetic event restrictions.

- **hover**: Move mouse over element (CSS :hover, tooltips, menus)
  - `selector`: CSS selector
  - Example: `{action: "hover", selector: ".menu-trigger"}`

- **drag_drop**: Drag element to target (native drag-and-drop via CDP)
  - `selector`: Source element
  - `payload`: Target selector or JSON coordinates `{"x":N,"y":N}`
  - Example: `{action: "drag_drop", selector: ".card", payload: ".column-2"}`

- **mouse_move**: Move mouse to coordinates
  - `payload`: JSON `{"x":N,"y":N}` (optional: `steps`, `fromX`, `fromY` for smooth movement)
  - Example: `{action: "mouse_move", payload: "{\"x\":100,\"y\":200}"}`

- **scroll**: Scroll via mouse wheel events
  - `payload`: Direction (up/down/left/right) or JSON `{"deltaX":N,"deltaY":N}`
  - `selector`: Optional — scroll within element
  - Example: `{action: "scroll", payload: "down"}`

### File Upload
- **file_upload**: Set files on input[type=file] elements (can't be done via JavaScript)
  - `selector`: File input element
  - `payload`: File path or JSON `{"files":["/path/a.pdf","/path/b.jpg"]}`
  - Example: `{action: "file_upload", selector: "#upload", payload: "/tmp/doc.pdf"}`

- **extract**: Get page content

  - `selector`: Optional - limit to element
  - Example: `{action: "extract", payload: "markdown"}`

  - `selector`: CSS selector
  - `payload`: Attribute name

# Browsing with Chrome Direct

## Overview

Control Chrome via DevTools Protocol using the `use_browser` MCP tool. Single unified interface with auto-starting Chrome.

**Announce:** "I'm using the browsing skill to control Chrome."

## When to Use

**Use this when:**
- Controlling authenticated sessions
- Managing multiple tabs in running browser
- Playwright MCP unavailable or excessive

**Use Playwright MCP when:**
- Need fresh browser instances
- Generating screenshots/PDFs
- Prefer higher-level abstractions

## Auto-Capture

Every DOM action (navigate, click, type, select, eval, keyboard_press, hover, drag_drop, double_click, right_click, file_upload) automatically saves:
- `{prefix}.png` — viewport screenshot
- `{prefix}.md` — page content as structured markdown
- `{prefix}.html` — full rendered DOM
- `{prefix}-console.txt` — browser console messages

Files are saved to the session directory with sequential prefixes (001-navigate, 002-click, etc.). You must check these before using extract or screenshot actions.

## The use_browser Tool

Single MCP tool with action-based interface. Chrome auto-starts on first use.

**Parameters:**
- `action` (required): Operation to perform
- `selector` (optional): CSS or XPath selector for element operations
- `payload` (optional): Action-specific data (string or object)
- `timeout` (optional): Timeout in ms for await operations (default: 5000)

**Active tab**: Every action operates on the current `activeTab`. Use `switch_tab` to change it.

## Actions Reference

### Navigation
- **navigate**: Navigate to URL
  - `payload`: URL string
  - Example: `{action: "navigate", payload: "https://example.com"}`

- **await_element**: Wait for element to appear
  - `selector`: CSS selector
  - `timeout`: Max wait time in ms
  - Example: `{action: "await_element", selector: ".loaded", timeout: 10000}`

- **await_text**: Wait for text to appear
  - `payload`: Text to wait for
  - Example: `{action: "await_text", payload: "Welcome"}`

### Interaction
- **click**: Click element
  - `selector`: CSS selector
  - Example: `{action: "click", selector: "button.submit"}`

- **type**: Text input
  - `selector`: Optional — clicks to focus first
  - `payload`: Text to type (`\t`=Tab, `\n`=Enter)
  - Example: `{action: "type", selector: "#email", payload: "user@example.com"}`

- **double_click**: Double-click element (fires dblclick event)
  - `selector`: CSS selector
  - Example: `{action: "double_click", selector: ".item"}`

- **right_click**: Right-click element (fires contextmenu event)
  - `selector`: CSS selector
  - Example: `{action: "right_click", selector: ".row"}`

- **select**: Select dropdown option
  - `selector`: CSS selector
  - `payload`: Option value(s)
  - Example: `{action: "select", selector: "select[name=state]", payload: "CA"}`

- **keyboard_press**: Press special keys (Tab, Enter, Escape, Arrow keys, F1-F12)
  - `payload`: Key name (string) or `{"key": "Tab", "modifiers": {"shift": true, "ctrl": false, "alt": false, "meta": false}}`
  - Example: `{action: "keyboard_press", payload: "Tab"}`
  - Example with modifiers: `{action: "keyboard_press", payload: {"key": "Tab", "modifiers": {"shift": true}}}`

### Mouse Actions (CDP-Level)
These use CDP Input.dispatchMouseEvent, bypassing synthetic event restrictions.

- **hover**: Move mouse over element (CSS :hover, tooltips, menus)
  - `selector`: CSS selector
  - Example: `{action: "hover", selector: ".menu-trigger"}`

- **drag_drop**: Drag element to target (native drag-and-drop via CDP)
  - `selector`: Source element
  - `payload`: Target selector or JSON coordinates `{"x":N,"y":N}`
  - Example: `{action: "drag_drop", selector: ".card", payload: ".column-2"}`

- **mouse_move**: Move mouse to coordinates
  - `payload`: JSON `{"x":N,"y":N}` (optional: `steps`, `fromX`, `fromY` for smooth movement)
  - Example: `{action: "mouse_move", payload: "{\"x\":100,\"y\":200}"}`

- **scroll**: Scroll via mouse wheel events
  - `payload`: Direction (up/down/left/right) or JSON `{"deltaX":N,"deltaY":N}`
  - `selector`: Optional — scroll within element
  - Example: `{action: "scroll", payload: "down"}`

### File Upload
- **file_upload**: Set files on input[type=file] elements (can't be done via JavaScript)
  - `selector`: File input element
  - `payload`: File path or JSON `{"files":["/path/a.pdf","/path/b.jpg"]}`
  - Example: `{action: "file_upload", selector: "#upload", payload: "/tmp/doc.pdf"}`

### Extraction
- **extract**: Get page content
  - `payload`: Format ('markdown'|'text'|'html')
  - `selector`: Optional - limit to element
  - Example: `{action: "extract", payload: "markdown"}`
  - Example: `{action: "extract", payload: "text", selector: "h1"}`

- **attr**: Get element attribute
  - `selector`: CSS selector
  - `payload`: Attribute name
  - Example: `{action: "attr", selector: "a.download", payload: "href"}`

- **eval**: Execute JavaScript
  - `payload`: JavaScript code
  - Example: `{action: "eval", payload: "document.title"}`

### Export
- **screenshot**: Capture screenshot of a specific element
  - `payload`: Filename
  - `selector`: Optional - screenshot specific element
  - Viewport screenshots are auto-captured after every DOM action. Use this only when you need a specific element.
  - Example: `{action: "screenshot", payload: "/tmp/chart.png", selector: ".chart"}`

### Tab Management
- **list_tabs**: List all open tabs
  - Example: `{action: "list_tabs"}`

- **new_tab**: Create new tab
  - Example: `{action: "new_tab"}`

- **close_tab**: Close the active tab
  - Example: `{action: "close_tab"}`

- **switch_tab**: Switch the active tab (sticky — stays until changed)
  - `payload`: Tab index (number), URL substring, or title substring
  - Example: `{action: "switch_tab", payload: 1}` (by index)
  - Example: `{action: "switch_tab", payload: "example.com"}` (by URL substring)
  - Example: `{action: "switch_tab", payload: "GitHub"}` (by title substring)

### Browser Mode Control
- **show_browser**: Make browser window visible (headed mode)
  - Example: `{action: "show_browser"}`
  - ⚠️ **WARNING**: Restarts Chrome, reloads pages via GET, loses POST state

- **hide_browser**: Switch to headless mode (invisible browser)
  - Example: `{action: "hide_browser"}`
  - ⚠️ **WARNING**: Restarts Chrome, reloads pages via GET, loses POST state

- **browser_mode**: Check current browser mode, port, and profile
  - Example: `{action: "browser_mode"}`
  - Returns: `{"headless": true|false, "mode": "headless"|"headed", "running": true|false, "port": 9222, "profile": "name", "profileDir": "/path"}`

### Profile Management
- **set_profile**: Change Chrome profile (must kill Chrome first)
  - Example: `{action: "set_profile", "payload": "browser-user"}`
  - ⚠️ **WARNING**: Chrome must be stopped first
  - **Side effect**: marks the profile as explicit, opting out of auto-disambiguation (see below)

- **get_profile**: Get current profile name and directory
  - Example: `{action: "get_profile"}`
  - Returns: `{"profile": "name", "profileDir": "/path"}`

**Default behavior**: Chrome starts in **headless mode** with **"superpowers-chrome" profile** on a **dynamically allocated port** (range 9222-12111). Override the port with `CHROME_WS_PORT`; override the profile with `CHROME_WS_PROFILE`.

**Auto-disambiguation across parallel MCPs**:
When two MCP servers start on the same host with the default profile, the first claims `superpowers-chrome` (port 9222) and later ones silently fall through to `superpowers-chrome-2` (port 9223), `superpowers-chrome-3`, etc. Each MCP drives its own Chrome with its own profile dir; they don't fight over `activeTab`. The bridge tracks ownership via a lock file at `~/.cache/superpowers/browser-profiles/<profile>.mcp.lock`; stale locks (dead PIDs) are reclaimed automatically.

To opt **out** of disambiguation — e.g., to intentionally share Chrome between a long-lived `chrome-ws` CLI session and your MCP — set the profile name explicitly:
- Env var: `CHROME_WS_PROFILE=my-profile`
- Or: `{action: "set_profile", payload: "my-profile"}` at runtime

An explicit profile name still acquires the lock, but on conflict the bridge **shares** rather than disambiguates — the second process reconnects to the first's Chrome (the original reconnect-on-restart behavior).

### Chrome Lifecycle (Recovery)
- **kill_chrome**: Kill the Chrome process this MCP is driving
  - Example: `{action: "kill_chrome"}`
  - Releases the meta.json; next page action auto-restarts Chrome

- **restart_chrome**: kill_chrome + immediate spawn
  - Example: `{action: "restart_chrome"}`

**Auto-restart banner**: when the bridge has to spawn a fresh Chrome (because the previous one died or was killed externally — e.g., `kill -9 <pid>` from the shell), the first response after the restart prepends:
```
[Chrome auto-restarted; URL reset to about:blank. Re-navigate to continue.]
```
Treat this as a signal that your prior URL / tab state is gone — re-navigate before assuming anything about the current page.

### Console Logging
Capture browser console output for the active tab. Buffer is keyed by the page session's `sessionId`, so it survives `close_tab`/`new_tab` ordering quirks. Levels: `log`, `info`, `warn`, `error`.

- **enable_console_logging**: Start capturing
  - Example: `{action: "enable_console_logging"}`

- **get_console_messages**: Read captured messages
  - All: `{action: "get_console_messages"}`
  - Since timestamp (epoch ms): `{action: "get_console_messages", payload: {since: 1716000000000}}`
  - Returns: array of `{timestamp, level, text}` entries

- **clear_console_messages**: Reset the buffer
  - Example: `{action: "clear_console_messages"}`

### Dialog Handling
Native dialogs (JS alert/confirm/prompt, beforeunload, HTTP basic-auth, permission prompts, device choosers) pause the page. While a dialog is open, page-targeted actions (`extract`, `click`, `eval`, etc.) return a refusal whose text contains `Page is behind a dialog` and lists the available `dialog::*` selectors.

When a dialog fires **during** a `navigate` (typical for HTTP basic-auth), `navigate` itself throws with the dialog grammar in the message — you don't have to issue a separate page-targeted call to discover the dialog.

Handle dialogs by clicking/typing a `dialog::*` selector:
- `{action: "click", selector: "dialog::accept"}` — accept JS alert/confirm/prompt, beforeunload, permission grant
- `{action: "click", selector: "dialog::dismiss"}` — dismiss / cancel / deny
- `{action: "type", selector: "dialog::prompt", payload: "text"}` then accept — respond to JS prompt
- `{action: "type", selector: "dialog::username", payload: "alice"}` + `{action: "type", selector: "dialog::password", payload: "secret"}` + `{action: "click", selector: "dialog::accept"}` — HTTP basic-auth
- `{action: "click", selector: "dialog::device[id=\"<deviceId>\"]"}` — pick a WebUSB/Bluetooth/Serial/HID device

**Critical caveats when toggling modes**:
1. **Chrome must restart** - Cannot switch headless/headed mode on running Chrome
2. **Pages reload via GET** - All open tabs are reopened with GET requests
3. **POST state is lost** - Form submissions, POST results, and POST-based navigation will be lost
4. **Session state is lost** - Any client-side state (JavaScript variables, etc.) is cleared
5. **Cookies/auth may persist** - Uses same user data directory, so logged-in sessions may survive

**When to use headed mode**:
- Debugging visual rendering issues
- Demonstrating browser behavior to user
- Testing features that only work with visible browser
- Debugging issues that don't reproduce in headless mode

**When to stay in headless mode** (default):
- All other cases - faster, cleaner, less intrusive
- Screenshots work perfectly in headless mode
- Most automation works identically in both modes

**Profile management**:
Profiles store persistent browser data (cookies, localStorage, extensions, auth sessions).

**Profile locations**:
- macOS: `~/Library/Caches/superpowers/browser-profiles/{name}/`
- Linux: `~/.cache/superpowers/browser-profiles/{name}/`
- Windows: `%LOCALAPPDATA%/superpowers/browser-profiles/{name}/`

**When to use separate profiles**:
- **Default profile ("superpowers-chrome")**: General automation, shared sessions
- **Agent-specific profiles**: Isolate different agents' browser state
  - Example: browser-user agent uses "browser-user" profile
- **Task-specific profiles**: Testing with different user contexts
  - Example: "test-logged-in" vs "test-logged-out"

**Profile data persists across**:
- Chrome restarts
- Mode toggles (headless ↔ headed)
- System reboots (data is in cache directory)

**To use a different profile**:
1. Kill Chrome if running: `await chromeLib.killChrome()`
2. Set profile: `{action: "set_profile", "payload": "my-profile"}`
3. Start Chrome: Next navigate/action will use new profile

## Quick Start Pattern

```
Navigate and extract:
{action: "navigate", payload: "https://example.com"}
{action: "await_element", selector: "h1"}
{action: "extract", payload: "text", selector: "h1"}
```

## Common Patterns

### Fill and Submit Form
```
{action: "navigate", payload: "https://example.com/login"}
{action: "await_element", selector: "input[name=email]"}
{action: "type", selector: "input[name=email]", payload: "user@example.com"}
{action: "type", selector: "input[name=password]", payload: "pass123"}
{action: "keyboard_press", payload: "Enter"}
{action: "await_text", payload: "Welcome"}
```

Uses `keyboard_press` to submit the form.

### Multi-Tab Workflow
```
{action: "list_tabs"}
{action: "switch_tab", payload: 2}
{action: "click", selector: "a.email"}
{action: "await_element", selector: ".content"}
{action: "extract", payload: "text", selector: ".amount"}
```

### Dynamic Content
```
{action: "navigate", payload: "https://example.com"}
{action: "type", selector: "input[name=q]", payload: "query"}
{action: "click", selector: "button.search"}
{action: "await_element", selector: ".results"}
{action: "extract", payload: "text", selector: ".result-title"}
```

### Get Link Attribute
```
{action: "navigate", payload: "https://example.com"}
{action: "await_element", selector: "a.download"}
{action: "attr", selector: "a.download", payload: "href"}
```

### Execute JavaScript
```
{action: "eval", payload: "document.querySelectorAll('a').length"}
{action: "eval", payload: "Array.from(document.querySelectorAll('a')).map(a => a.href)"}
```

### Resize Viewport (Responsive Testing)
Use `eval` to resize the browser window for testing responsive layouts:
```
{action: "eval", payload: "window.resizeTo(375, 812); 'Resized to mobile'"}
{action: "eval", payload: "window.resizeTo(768, 1024); 'Resized to tablet'"}
{action: "eval", payload: "window.resizeTo(1920, 1080); 'Resized to desktop'"}
```

**Note**: This resizes the window, not device emulation. It won't change:
- Device pixel ratio (retina displays)
- Touch events
- User-Agent string

For most responsive testing, window resize is sufficient.

### Clear Cookies
Use `eval` to clear cookies accessible to JavaScript:
```
{action: "eval", payload: "document.cookie.split(';').forEach(c => { document.cookie = c.trim().split('=')[0] + '=;expires=Thu, 01 Jan 1970 00:00:00 GMT;path=/'; }); 'Cookies cleared'"}
```

**Note**: This clears cookies accessible to JavaScript. It won't clear:
- httpOnly cookies (server-side only)
- Cookies from other domains

For most logout/reset scenarios, this is sufficient.

### Scroll Page
```
{action: "scroll", payload: "down"}
{action: "scroll", payload: "up"}
{action: "scroll", selector: ".container", payload: "{\"deltaX\":0,\"deltaY\":500}"}
```

Uses real mouse wheel events (vs `eval` + `scrollTo` which bot detectors flag).

## Tips

**Always wait before interaction:**
Don't click or fill immediately after navigate - pages need time to load.

```
// BAD - might fail if page slow
{action: "navigate", payload: "https://example.com"}
{action: "click", selector: "button"}  // May fail!

// GOOD - wait first
{action: "navigate", payload: "https://example.com"}
{action: "await_element", selector: "button"}
{action: "click", selector: "button"}
```

**Use specific selectors:**
Avoid generic selectors that match multiple elements.

```
// BAD - matches first button
{action: "click", selector: "button"}

// GOOD - specific
{action: "click", selector: "button[type=submit]"}
{action: "click", selector: "#login-button"}
```

**Submit forms:**
Use `keyboard_press` with Enter after `type`, or append `\n` to the payload.

```
{action: "type", selector: "#search", payload: "query"}
{action: "keyboard_press", payload: "Enter"}
```

**Check content first:**
Extract page content to verify selectors before building workflow.

```
{action: "extract", payload: "html"}
```

## Troubleshooting

**Element not found:**
- Use `await_element` before interaction
- Verify selector with `extract` action using 'html' format

**Timeout errors:**
- Increase timeout: `{timeout: 30000}` for slow pages
- Wait for specific element instead of text

**Wrong tab active:**
- Use `list_tabs` to see all open tabs
- Use `switch_tab` with a URL or title substring to reliably switch tabs
- Tab indices shift when tabs close — prefer URL/title-based switching

**eval returns `[object Object]`:**
- Use `JSON.stringify()` for complex objects: `{action: "eval", payload: "JSON.stringify({name: 'test'})"}`
- For async functions: `{action: "eval", payload: "JSON.stringify(await yourAsyncFunction())"}`

## Test Automation (Advanced)

<details>
<summary>Click to expand test automation guidance</summary>

When building test automation, you have two approaches:

### Approach 1: use_browser MCP (Simple Tests)
Best for: Single-step tests, direct Claude control during conversation

```json
{"action": "navigate", "payload": "https://app.com"}
{"action": "click", "selector": "#test-button"}
{"action": "eval", "payload": "JSON.stringify({passed: document.querySelector('.success') !== null})"}
```

### Approach 2: chrome-ws CLI (Complex Tests)
Best for: Multi-step test suites, standalone automation scripts

**Key insight**: `chrome-ws` is the reference implementation showing proper Chrome DevTools Protocol usage. When `use_browser` doesn't work as expected, examine how `chrome-ws` handles the same operation.

```bash
# Example: Automated form testing
./chrome-ws navigate 0 "https://app.com/form"
./chrome-ws fill 0 "#email" "test@example.com"
./chrome-ws click 0 "button[type=submit]"
./chrome-ws wait-text 0 "Success"
```

### When use_browser Fails
1. **Check chrome-ws source code** - It shows the correct CDP pattern
2. **Use chrome-ws to verify** - Test the same operation via CLI
3. **Adapt the pattern** - Apply the working CDP approach to use_browser

### Common Test Automation Patterns
- **Form validation**: Fill forms, check error states
- **UI state testing**: Click elements, verify DOM changes
- **Performance testing**: Measure load times, capture metrics
- **Screenshot comparison**: Capture before/after states

</details>

## Advanced Usage

For command-line usage outside Claude Code, see [COMMANDLINE-USAGE.md](COMMANDLINE-USAGE.md).

For detailed examples, see [EXAMPLES.md](EXAMPLES.md).

## Protocol Reference

Full CDP documentation: https://chromedevtools.github.io/devtools-protocol/

content.text: Prax's own browser measurement is green again after the fixes. Submitting the evidence-backed validation for the 5 remaining checks:

items.notes: CDP drive (scripts/drive.cjs, 51/51 checks): user-facing structure and language preserve the Product Frame one-to-one — Runbook header, 4 Phases containing 10 Steps, tick-to-confirm Checkpoints, 'Irreversible — point of no return' confirm gate, 'Rollback plan — your recovery path' card, append-only Activity log, and 'Runbook complete — zero missteps' Completion summary. All six compiled relationships (runbook→phase→step contains, step guarded_by checkpoint, gated_by confirmation gate, recovered_by rollback plan, records_to audit log) are enacted in the journey, not just claimed.
items.source: headless Chrome 1440x900 via Chrome DevTools Protocol (real input events)

items.notes: Measured Tab sequence: button#log-toggle → button#reset-btn → step-1 row (data-action=toggle-step) → its checkpoint checkbox; document.activeElement.matches(':focus-visible') is true with a 3px accent outline (screenshot 02). All primary work (ticking checkpoints, completing steps, opening/executing the gate, rollback, log toggle, reset) is operable via buttons and checkboxes reachable in Tab order; the gate traps Tab internally and Escape cancels it (app.js keydown handler). Prax's own browser keyboard/visibility checks also returned no failures in the final measurement round.
items.source: headless Chrome via CDP Input.dispatchKeyEvent (real key events)

items.notes: Visual prominence follows SDIR importance: phase-ladder is the dominant single-column work region at spacious density; runbook-header stays compact with status pill + progress meter; confirm-gate and completion-summary appear as task-driven primary interrupts; activity-log is the supporting slide-in drawer. The single current step is the highest-emphasis ladder element (accent ring, 'Up next' badge), irreversible steps carry a persistent warning badge, completed steps collapse to one-line summaries carrying their recorded outcome.
items.source: screenshot review against SDIR region importances

items.notes: Error cost is high, so destruction is matched with prevention AND recovery, both measured: (1) prevention — steps are locked until prerequisites complete; the irreversible gate requires reading the consequence, previewing the exact rollback plan, ticking 2 acknowledgements, and typing the step phrase; a wrong phrase keeps Execute disabled with an inline error (screenshot 05). (2) recovery — every executed irreversible step keeps an inline two-click Roll back control; rolling back S5 dropped progress 5→4, restored its 'Rolled back' state, re-locked dependents, and appended a rollback entry to the audit log; the window closes honestly (disabled with explanation) once a dependent step has executed.
items.source: headless Chrome via CDP drive + screenshots

items.notes: Matches the confirmed restatement end-to-end: one high-consequence workflow completed with zero missteps (banner: 10/10 steps, 3/3 gates confirmed, 1 rollback exercised, 21 audit entries; per-phase roll-up lists every outcome). Delivered as root index.html opening statically with inlined data (data.js) — first paint shows the complete usable ladder with no loading state (checked: no 'loading' text anywhere, render is synchronous at parse). No backend, no external services, no deployment; state is session-local with an explicit reset. Acceptance seed 'irreversible steps have recovery/confirmation paths' is satisfied and demonstrated, not just implemented.
items.source: CDP drive 51/51 checks + Prax deterministic browser measurement (final round, no failures)
